clue.text: Positionally, the word "flexible" has ___ , I see? That's what it is!

definitions.text: Positionally, the word "flexible" has ___ , I see? That's what it is!

parts.note: fill the gap so the sentence describes the word's spelling: its final letter is E, so it has E in the last position
taken as written
the word see is spoken just like the letter C

explanation.surface: A coy remark about the word flexible, ending with a triumphant 'that's what it is'.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the gap as a description of the spelling of flexible: it has E LAST. Then 'I see' sounds out I and C, and the whole sentence names a synonym of flexible.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flexible stretches and springs back, which is the core sense of being stretchy or pliant.

clue.text: At all centres, sweaty brassieres analysed just like that!

indicators.note: every one of the three following words gives up only its central pair of letters

explanation.surface: Sweaty bras have been put under scientific scrutiny, it seems, with a flippant shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word gives its middle two letters: EA from sweaty, SI from brassieres, LY from analysed.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something 'just like that' means doing it without effort, with no trouble at all.

clue.text: After a chorus is opposed?

indicators.note: the song section is placed after the letter A, so it follows in the answer

parts.note: taken as written
a song's chorus alternates with its verse, so the clue word leads to the other section of a song

explanation.surface: A question about whether a singer is against something once the refrain is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface joke is that a verse comes after a chorus in a song; cryptically, VERSE comes after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being opposed to something means having a strong dislike of or objection to it.

clue.text: Entering wood, a king and woolly bear have a cuppa, perhaps?

indicators.note: the king and the jumbled animal go into the timber word, splitting it after its first letter

parts.note: teak is a hardwood
taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: woolly means fuzzy or muddled, so the letters of bear are mixed up

explanation.surface: A monarch and a shaggy bear wander into a forest and sit down for tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woolly' scrambles the animal's letters to EABR. 'Entering' puts the king, the A and those letters inside the wood. A cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Stopping work for a cup of tea is a typical example of pausing to rest.

clue.text: Under surface of compost, dig deeply for aromatic bud

indicators.note: in a down entry the second piece sits beneath the first letter
the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it, and liking it deeply is to love it

explanation.surface: A gardening tip: get below the top layer of compost and dig hard to find a fragrant bud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dig' looks like a gardening verb but is slang for like, so 'dig deeply' is LOVE, placed under C.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tropical tree, used as a fragrant spice.

clue.text: See 12
Footballers' July, when there was no water on?

parts.note: a time before the oceans existed would be pre-seas
taken as written

explanation.surface: A summer month for players, oddly described as a time without any water about.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as PRE-SEAS-ON: a time before the seas. In Britain, July is when football clubs train and play friendlies before the league begins.
explanation.definitionFit: July is the warm-up month before the English football league begins in August, the period before competition starts.

clue.text: Food content of an alphabet 24, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the letters are spoken out loud to give the answer

parts.note: 24 is SOUP, and alphabet soup holds pasta letters, among them some P's

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what goes into a child's alphabet soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 is the answer SOUP; the letters floating in alphabet soup include P's, which spoken sound like a green vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Peas are a common vegetable eaten as food, so the general word covers them.

clue.text: Is the president a degree less affluent? That's not entirely suggesting consistent pressure

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the academic qualification is taken away from the president's name

parts.note: Barack Obama was the US president when this puzzle appeared
MA, Master of Arts, is a degree

indicators.note: only part of the word is used, its final letter dropped

parts.note: affluent means rich

explanation.surface: A satirical question about whether the president has become poorer by a degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' strips MA from OBAMA to leave OBA; 'not entirely' cuts RICH to RIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Isobaric lines on a weather map join points of equal atmospheric pressure, so the word implies uniform pressure.

clue.text: Among grass, something flat getting lost

indicators.note: the flat object goes inside the informing verb

parts.note: to grass is British slang for informing on someone, as is to sing
a tray is a flat carrier

explanation.surface: Something flat has gone missing in the long grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' looks like the lawn but is the British slang verb for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Straying means wandering off course, which is how something gets lost.

clue.text: Reported pale food

indicators.note: reported signals a word said out loud that sounds like the answer

parts.note: a pale is a fence post or stake

explanation.surface: Someone has been told about some colourless food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pale' seems to describe the food but is a noun, a fence post.
explanation.definitionFit: Steak is a thick slice of beef, a familiar dish.

clue.text: Finally, once or twice, page-turning Cosi Fan fan?

indicators.note: turning means the collected letters are spun round into a new order
only the last letter of once is taken
the little word or is written out two times

explanation.surface: A fan of the Mozart opera flicks through the score once or twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' gives E from once, 'twice' gives OROR, and 'turning' shuffles E, OROR and PAGE together. Cosi fan tutte is a Mozart opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keen on the Mozart work Cosi fan tutte is a fan who attends performances at the opera house.

clue.text: A dose of Ebola's safe? Very contagious disease!

indicators.note: dose of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A doubtful health question about whether Ebola is safe, answered with an alarmed exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic illness of West Africa that spreads between people.

clue.text: 24 a 19 20 1 across 21 6 15, say — from this?

parts.note: read the cross-referenced answers aloud in order and they sound out the famous long nonsense word, which comes from a Disney film

explanation.surface: A string of grid answers is offered as a quotation, and the solver asks where it comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: The answers are SOUP, A, COLLIE, FRIDGE, ELASTIC, EGGS, PEAS, HALITOSIS: spoken together they sound like the made-up word from the 1964 film's song.
explanation.definitionFit: The nanny of P. L. Travers's books, played by Julie Andrews, sings the song with that nonsense word in the Disney film.

clue.text: Player, brilliant player cut short, in essence

indicators.note: the shortened performer goes inside the word for substance

parts.note: the content of something is its substance or essence

indicators.note: the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: a star is a brilliant performer

explanation.surface: A competitor described as a brilliant player whose career was cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the final letter of the star; 'in' places the rest inside the word for essence, after its E.
explanation.definitionFit: A contestant is anyone taking part in a game or competition, a participant.

clue.text: This peak's claimed by old heretic for the master of the works?

indicators.note: the other pieces are taken into the heretic's name, held inside it

parts.note: an Arian followed Arius, whose fourth-century teaching was condemned as heresy
taken as written
a tor is a rocky hilltop, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A mountain is seized by an ancient heretic, and someone asks who is in charge of the works.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the old masters and their works: someone who studies them is the expert on such masterpieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar of paintings and sculpture is an expert on the old masters' works, so knows them thoroughly.

clue.text: Relative beneath headlight inhaling it, not a breath of fresh air

definitions.text: not a breath of fresh air

indicators.note: in a down entry the relative sits below the rest
the small word is taken inside, as breath is drawn in

parts.note: a halo is a ring of light around the head
taken as written
sis is short for sister

explanation.surface: A family member under a car's headlamp breathes in fumes, hardly fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'headlight' looks like a car lamp but means a light round the head; in this down clue 'beneath' puts the relative at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad breath is the opposite of a pleasant, fresh exhalation, hence the playful understatement.

clue.text: Treat a foot breaking three times, getting old

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the foot word splits up the three Ts, going between them

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, so three times give three Ts
the foot of something is its end

explanation.surface: A doctor treats a foot that has broken three times as the patient gets older.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot' looks medical but is END, which breaks into TTT as TT END T.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend to a patient or a problem is to deal with it or care for it.

clue.text: Double deoxygenated gas exploding in bum

indicators.note: an explosion scatters things, so the letters are blown into a new order
oxygen's chemical symbol O is removed from the word

explanation.surface: A chemistry mishap: twice the deoxygenated gas goes off in someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deoxygenated' drops O from Double to leave DUBLE; 'exploding' scrambles DUBLE with GAS. Bum is British slang for a layabout as well as a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazybones who lies in bed late is a loafer or idler, in slang a good-for-nothing.

clue.text: Discuss in some detail setting out the gallant knight's limits

indicators.note: setting out suggests arranging afresh, so the letters are rearranged
the edges of the word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A chivalrous knight sets off on a quest, and someone describes his boundaries at length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limits' gives KT from knight's; 'setting out' rearranges THE GALLANT plus KT.
explanation.definitionFit: To go into a subject at length is to talk about it fully and with plenty of particulars.

clue.text: Dog that's mine, untracked?

indicators.note: the railway abbreviation is removed, leaving the pit without rails

parts.note: a colliery is a coal mine

explanation.surface: An owner's dog has got loose and left no trail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' looks like a possessive but is a coal pit, COLLIERY; RY, short for railway, is the track taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: The collie is a sheepdog breed from Scotland, a working dog.

clue.text: Beginning to feel on edge, getting cooler

indicators.note: in a down entry, the first piece sits on top of the second
only the opening letter of feel is used

parts.note: a ridge is a raised edge or crest

explanation.surface: Someone starting to feel nervous gets calmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on edge' reads as nervous, but 'on' places F above RIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A refrigerator keeps food chilled, so it is a cooler in the household sense.

clue.text: Less peeled skin for horse food?

indicators.note: the peeled letters wrap round the horse word like a skin
a peeled word loses its outer letters, leaving its core

parts.note: gee-gee is a child's word for horse, abbreviated GG

explanation.surface: Less peeled skin is used as horse feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peeled' strips Less to ES, which then surrounds GG, the nursery horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggs, laid by hens, are an everyday food.

clue.text: Knockers are wobbly — and sore, too!

indicators.note: wobbly means shaky, so the letters are unsteadily rearranged

explanation.surface: A bawdy complaint about a sore, wobbly chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knockers' suggests the bawdy slang but means people knocking, who stand at the threshold.
explanation.definitionFit: People who knock are standing at the entrance to someone's house, which this phrase describes.

clue.text: Vacillating poet?

definitions.meaning: someone who wavers says no, then yes
Alfred ... was the English poet of The Highwayman

explanation.definitionFit: The two words joined sum up dithering, and they also make the surname of an English poet.

clue.text: Food not taken down then?

parts.note: so can mean then, as in 'so you agree'
something not taken down is still up

explanation.surface: A question about some food that never got put away.
explanation.definitionFit: A broth or liquid dish is a familiar food served in a bowl.

clue.text: In a questionable manner, call promissory note deceitful

parts.note: to dub someone is to call them by a name
an IOU is a written promise to pay
sly means sneaky and deceitful

explanation.surface: Someone labels an IOU dishonest in a shady way.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a doubtful or suspicious way is acting with questionable motives.

clue.text: Smith knocked over, was sick

indicators.note: something knocked over is turned the other way, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Delia Smith is a famous British TV cookery writer

explanation.surface: A smith was knocked over and felt ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smith' looks like a surname or a blacksmith but means the cook Delia Smith, whose first name is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To have ailed is to have been unwell or suffering from illness.

clue.text: Solver's companion is seizing up, coming across as complex character

parts.note: the Oxford English Dictionary, OED, is a crossword solver's reference

indicators.note: the two letters is grab hold of the next word, holding it inside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in an across entry the word up cannot point upward, so it is turned round to read right to left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword solver's helper seizes up when faced with a complicated figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming across' reads the little word backwards as PU. 'complex character' refers to the Freudian complex named after the mythical king.
explanation.definitionFit: The Theban king who unknowingly married his mother gave his name to Freud's famous psychological complex.

clue.text: That'll teach you it's different in the Home Counties!

indicators.note: the word for different goes inside the regional abbreviation

parts.note: the Home Counties around London are in the South East, abbreviated SE
other means different

explanation.surface: Someone smugly says things are done differently around London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London, in England's South East.
explanation.definitionFit: This childish retort of triumph is said when someone gets a comeuppance, like a told-you-so.
